title: Pied beauty
hookLine: a Jesuit thanks God for freckles and fickle things, then ends on a beauty past change (Pied Beauty)
tomorrow: a falcon hangs on the wind. why is the priest's heart hiding?

lines: GLORY BE TO GOD FOR DAPPLED THINGS.
WHY END ON WHAT DOESN'T CHANGE?
cards: Phone filters smooth every freckle off a face. A Jesuit priest named Gerard Manley Hopkins went the other way. His poem opens like a church prayer: "Glory be to God for dappled things".

Then it thanks God for skies patched like a cow's hide, the spots on a trout, finches' wings, and, stranger still, for "Whatever is fickle, freckled (who knows how?)". Fickle? Who thanks God for fickle?
And why does a poem crammed with things that keep changing end on someone who doesn't change at all?

teach.h: A JESUIT: TO THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD.
teach.b: Start with his training. Hopkins was a Jesuit, a member of the order whose motto is to the greater glory of God.

Jesuits are trained through the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola, and the Exercises begin with a foundation: people are made to praise, reverence and serve God, and the other things on the face of the earth are made to help them.
Hopkins looked hard at those other things.

teach.h: INSCAPE: WHAT MAKES A THING ITSELF.
teach.b: In his journals he used his own word, inscape, for the pattern that makes each thing itself and nothing else. Now the puzzle solves itself. The trout gives glory by being spotted.
The finch, by its wings. Even the odd ones, in his words "All things counter, original, spare, strange", give glory by being exactly what they are.
Then the turn: "He fathers-forth whose beauty is past change: / Praise him."
All the changing, freckled things come from a beauty that doesn't change.
The poem opens on glory and closes on praise, and some readers hear the old Jesuit habit of writing praise to God at the top and the bottom of a page.
That's the Catholic teaching under it: creation itself gives glory to God, and a creature praises by being what it was made to be. It's a roomy idea. Nothing has to be smoothed out first.
The freckle is part of the praise.

how: Jesuits pray through Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises, which begin with the Principle and Foundation; some retreat leaders read Pied Beauty aloud on a walk outdoors.

o: a painter's word for blending colors smoothly
the patched, spotted, many-colored beauty of things
the polished beauty of a flawless, made-up face

games.q: freckles and praise: tap the pairs.
p: a Jesuit priest who wrote Pied Beauty
the Exercises: people made to praise God
what makes a thing itself and nothing else
the beauty all dappled things come from

s: Pied Beauty praises only perfect, flawless things
it praises the dappled, the freckled, the fickle and the strange.
Hopkins was a Jesuit, trained in the Spiritual Exercises
and the Exercises begin with what people are made for: to praise, reverence and serve God.
the poem ends by saying all beauty fades
it ends on one whose beauty is past change: Praise him.

games.q: a friend wants every freckle edited out of her wedding photos. she asks what that dappled-things poem would say. what fits?
o: Hopkins thanks God for freckles; to him they're part of how a thing gives glory.
Hopkins would say smooth, perfect skin gives God the most glory.
Hopkins only meant nature: trout and finches, nothing human at all.
games.why: the poem praises whatever is fickle and freckled, and even all trades, their gear and tackle: human things are in it too.

practice: Find one dappled thing within reach: a leaf, a wood grain, a speckled stone, the back of your own hand. For two minutes, look at it the way Hopkins looked, every spot and streak and edge. Let it be exactly what it is.
The poem's last two words are there for anyone who wants them: praise him.

wordCard.voice: Pied beauty: Hopkins's title for the patched, spotted, mixed-up beauty of the world. Pied means patched in more than one color, and for him every patch gives glory.

orig.note: Latin: to the greater glory of God, the motto of the Jesuits, Hopkins's order.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: dappled things, every spot of them part of the praise. See you tomorrow.
